issues.legal_issue: A debtor holding an individually assessed share of an estate is an agriculturist when the assessment attributable to that share does not exceed the statutory disqualifying limit.
material_facts: The debtors held interests in two villages that formed an estate, but the properties were held in defined shares rather than jointly as ancestral property.
The estate's assessment had been apportioned between the villages, and the assessment attributable to each debtor's share was below the disqualifying limit.
issues.conclusion: The debtors were agriculturists and were entitled to seek scaling down of the debt on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(ii) and proviso (D) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, an agriculturist includes a person with a qualifying interest in agricultural land, while a landholder is excluded if the relevant assessment exceeds the statutory limit. The court treated the properties as separate interests and relied on C.N. Arunachala v. C.A. Muruganatha Mudaliar, [1954] S.C.R. 243, concerning the character of property taken under a will.

predicates.debt_scaling_application: The proceeding seeks to scale down a debt on the basis that the debtors are agriculturists.
predicates.land_interests_held_in_defined_shares: The debtors held defined individual interests in the relevant land rather than holding it jointly as one undivided interest.
predicates.assessment_attributable_to_each_share_be: The assessment attributable to each debtor's interest was below the limit that would disqualify a landholder from agriculturist status.

issues.definition: When a debt-scaling application concerns debtors with defined individual land interests and each interest's attributable assessment is below the disqualifying limit, the debtors are agriculturists.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court does not improperly interfere with a factual finding when it obtains evidence and a finding and then independently assesses that material before deciding the matter.
material_facts: In the revision proceeding, the High Court directed the trial court to take evidence and report whether the debtors were agriculturists.
The parties were given an opportunity to object to the reported finding, and the High Court considered the evidence before reaching its own conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not improperly interfering in revision with a trial court's finding of fact.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to the procedural circumstances before it: the High Court had called for evidence and a finding, subject to objections, and was entitled to examine that material and draw its own inference.

predicates.revision_proceeding: The matter is before a higher court in a revision proceeding.
predicates.reviewing_court_ordered_evidence_and_a_f: The reviewing court directed that evidence be taken and a finding be submitted for its consideration.
predicates.parties_could_object_to_the_finding: The parties had an opportunity to challenge the submitted finding before the reviewing court decided the matter.

issues.definition: In a revision proceeding, a reviewing court that has obtained evidence and a finding, with an opportunity for party objections, may assess that evidence without improperly interfering with a factual finding.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree that remained unexecuted or unsatisfied in part when the amending law commenced was subject to debt scaling, just as a decree passed after contest was.
material_facts: The debt decree was made by compromise before the amending law commenced.
Some payments had been made, but the decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced.
The debtors later applied to have the decree scaled down.
issues.conclusion: The application was governed by section 16(iii), read with section 19(2), and the compromise decree was subject to scaling down; amounts already paid or realized did not have to be refunded.
issues.legal_principle: Section 19(2) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as amended, and section 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, apply to decrees not executed or satisfied in full before the amending law commenced. The proviso protects creditors from having to refund sums already paid or realized. The court held that compromise decrees are not distinguished from decrees passed after contest for this purpose, and relied on Venkataratnam v. Seshamma, I.L.R. (1952) Mad. 492.

predicates.debt_scaling_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to scale down a debt embodied in a decree.
predicates.money_decree_unexecuted_or_partly_unsati: The money decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the relevant amending law commenced.

issues.definition: A money decree that remains unexecuted or partly unsatisfied when the relevant amending law commences is subject to scaling down in a debt-scaling proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A compromise decree does not create res judicata on an issue that the court did not decide.
material_facts: The debtors had previously sought scaling down in the original suit, but the suit ended in a compromise decree.
The court accepted the parties' agreement and did not decide whether the debtors qualified for scaling down.
The debtors later raised the issue in an application under the amended law.
issues.conclusion: The compromise decree did not operate as statutory or constructive res judicata and did not prevent the debtors from raising the issue again.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, res judicata requires a matter to have been heard and finally decided by a court; constructive res judicata likewise rests on a prior judicial decision. A compromise decree records the parties' agreement rather than a decision by the court. The court also recognized that the amended law conferred new rights to seek scaling down, subject to the terms of that law.

predicates.later_debt_scaling_proceeding: A later proceeding seeks debt scaling after an earlier decree was made.
predicates.earlier_compromise_decree: The earlier decree embodied an agreement accepted by the court.
predicates.earlier_judicial_determination_of_the_is: The court in the earlier proceeding actually decided the issue later raised.

issues.definition: When a later debt-scaling proceeding follows a compromise decree that did not include a judicial determination of the issue, the earlier decree does not bar the issue as res judicata.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rely on an alleged estoppel by conduct to defeat a later claim when that estoppel was not pleaded and tried.
material_facts: The decree-holders argued that the earlier compromise created an estoppel against the debtors.
They had not pleaded an estoppel by conduct, and the issue had not been tried on that basis.
There was evidence that some payments had been made under the compromise decree.
issues.conclusion: The court did not consider an estoppel by conduct because it had not been pleaded and tried; sums already paid were protected from refund by the statutory proviso.
issues.legal_principle: The court distinguished res judicata or estoppel by judgment from a possible estoppel arising from the parties' conduct. The latter required a plea and trial; the proviso to section 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, separately protected sums already paid or realized from a refund requirement.

predicates.later_debt_scaling_proceeding: A later proceeding seeks debt scaling after an earlier decree.
predicates.alleged_estoppel_based_on_party_conduct: A party asserts that the other party's conduct in the earlier dealings prevents the later claim.
predicates.conduct_estoppel_not_pleaded_and_tried: The alleged conduct-based estoppel was neither pleaded as an issue nor tried.

issues.definition: When conduct-based estoppel is asserted in a later debt-scaling proceeding but was not pleaded and tried, it cannot be relied on to defeat the claim.

issues.legal_issue: Debtors who qualify as agriculturists may obtain scaling down of a decree that remains subject to the amended debt-relief law, unless a legally sufficient bar prevents the claim.
material_facts: The debtors qualified as agriculturists because the assessment attributable to each of their defined shares was below the disqualifying limit.
The compromise decree had not been executed or satisfied in full when the amending law commenced.
The compromise did not amount to a judicial determination of the debtors' entitlement to scaling down, and no conduct-based estoppel had been pleaded and tried.
issues.conclusion: The debtors were entitled to have the decree scaled down, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(ii), 19(2), and 16(iii) of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act, 1938, as amended by the Madras Agriculturists Relief (Amendment) Act, 1948, entitled qualifying agriculturists to seek scaling down of an eligible decree. The court described the relief as protection for petty agriculturists from oppressive loans at usurious rates of interest and applied its rulings on agriculturist status, decrees not fully executed or satisfied, and res judicata.

rule.if: debt_scaling_proceeding and debtors_are_agriculturists and decree_is_subject_to_scaling_down and no_prior_judicial_bar_to_the_claim

predicates.debt_scaling_proceeding: The proceeding seeks to scale down a debt embodied in a decree.
predicates.debtors_are_agriculturists: The debtors meet the applicable criteria for agriculturist status.
predicates.decree_is_subject_to_scaling_down: The decree remains eligible for scaling down because it was not executed or satisfied in full when the relevant amending law commenced.
predicates.no_prior_judicial_bar_to_the_claim: No prior judicial determination bars the debtors from raising their claim to scaling down.

issues.definition: A debt-scaling proceeding results in entitlement to scaling down when the debtors are agriculturists, the decree remains eligible, and no prior judicial determination bars the claim.
